How the lighthouse keeper counted his staircase

By Mara Veld

Every evening for thirty-one years, Anders Holm climbed the same two hundred and four steps to the lamp room of the Skarvik light. He counted them aloud, not because he could forget the number, but because the counting kept the climb from feeling long.

The stairs themselves were cast in iron in 1893 and bolted into the granite by men who never saw the lamp lit. Each tread has a shallow dip worn by boots, and in the wet months the whole spiral sweats, so that the handrail is cold and slick under a palm.

What the steps taught him

When the automated lamp replaced the keepers, Holm was offered a pension and a flat in town. He took the pension and kept the stairs, walking up once a week with a thermos and a notebook, writing down the weather and the number of gulls on the gallery rail.

"A staircase is only a long sentence," he told the harbour board in his last meeting. "You read it one word at a time, and you do not skip."

Nobody climbs a lighthouse to arrive. They climb it to see how far the dark goes.

The notebooks now sit in the harbour museum, forty-one of them, filled with small upright handwriting and the occasional drawing of a gull. Visitors are allowed to turn the pages with cotton gloves, and most of them read for much longer than they planned to.
